intro: Test strategy and habits that keep a suite fast and trustworthy.

entries.short: Many unit, fewer integration, few end-to-end.
entries.medium: Unit tests are fast and pinpoint failures, integration tests cover the wiring, end-to-end tests cover the whole path. The shape is about cost and brittleness: inverting it produces a slow, flaky suite.
entries.detail: The trophy shape is a common refinement for frontend: fewer unit tests on implementation details, more integration tests, a few critical end-to-end flows.

entries.short: Assert on outcomes, not on internal calls.
entries.medium: A good test describes what the caller or user cares about, fails for one reason, and keeps passing when you refactor internals. If renaming a private method breaks it, it is testing the wrong thing.
entries.detail: Arrange, act, assert keeps it readable. Implementation-coupled tests are the main reason suites become a maintenance burden.

entries.short: Stub returns, spy records, mock expects, fake implements.
entries.medium: A fake, such as an in-memory database, exercises more real code than a mock while staying fast. Over-mocking produces tests that pass while the system is broken because they verify the interaction you wrote.
entries.detail: Reserve mocks for external services, time and randomness, and control those explicitly rather than mocking everything.

entries.short: Different scope, speed, confidence and failure signal.
entries.medium: Unit tests point at the exact failure but give low confidence in the system. Integration tests cover the seams. End-to-end tests tell you something is broken but not where, and are the most brittle.
entries.detail: Most bugs live at the seams, so a healthy suite is heavier on integration than the classic pyramid suggests.

entries.short: Passing and failing without a code change erodes trust.
entries.medium: Causes are timing and shared state: fixed sleeps, tests depending on order, real clocks and timezones, network calls, running animations. Wait for conditions with findBy or waitFor instead of sleeping.
entries.detail: Treat a flake as a bug. Re-running until green teaches the team to ignore red builds, and a real failure slips through.

entries.short: Red, green, refactor in short cycles.
entries.medium: Write the failing test first, make it pass with the simplest code, then refactor. Writing the test first designs the interface from the caller's point of view.
entries.detail: The red step matters: a test that has never failed might assert nothing. TDD shines on logic and bug fixes, and is awkward for exploratory UI work.

entries.medium: High coverage of trivial code proves nothing, and chasing a percentage leads to tests that assert nothing meaningful. Look at whether important paths and edge cases are covered instead.
entries.detail: Coverage is most useful for spotting whole modules that are never exercised.

entries.short: Inject a clock and seed randomness for determinism.
entries.medium: Real dates and Math.random make tests non-deterministic. Inject a clock, freeze the date, or seed the random source so the same input always produces the same output.
entries.detail: This is usually a smaller change than mocking the surrounding modules, and it keeps more of the real code under test.

entries.short: Await the result; never sleep and hope.
entries.medium: Return or await the promise so the framework knows when the test is done. For UI, use queries that retry until a timeout, such as findBy and waitFor, rather than asserting immediately after an action.
entries.detail: Forgetting to await is a classic source of false passes, where the test finishes before the assertion runs.

entries.short: Render and interact the way a user would.
entries.medium: Query by role and accessible name rather than by class or test id, so the test asserts on what a user perceives and doubles as an accessibility check. Fire real events and assert on visible output.
entries.detail: This is the frontend version of behaviour over implementation, and it catches missing labels and broken keyboard interaction along the way.

entries.short: Use a disposable real database, not a mocked one.
entries.medium: Integration tests should exercise the real query and constraints, so run them against a throwaway database, wrapped in a transaction that rolls back or reset between tests. Mocking the database hides the SQL bugs you most want to catch.
entries.detail: A test container gives a real engine per run, which is slower than a fake but catches migration, constraint and query errors.

entries.short: Run on every change and keep the signal honest.
entries.medium: Run the fast suite on every push and the slow end-to-end suite before merge. Fail the build on a red test and fix it promptly, or the suite stops being a gate.
entries.detail: Parallelise and shard as the suite grows, and cache dependencies so feedback stays in minutes.
